label: Artifact type, 'du' form
summary: Gives the French 'of the' word that goes before an artifact's type name: 'de la ', 'de l’' or 'du '.
details: Types such as animal hide, axe, brooch, ring, spear, dagger, goblet, jug, mace, panacea, philosopher's stone and tapestry get 'de la '. The armour kinds, bow, composite, elixir, longbow, pedestal, regalia, scientific apparatus and sword get 'de l’'. Any other type gets 'du '. FR_Le_ArtifactType sorts the same types into the same three groups and gives 'la ', 'l’' or 'le '. Runs on an artifact.

label: Artifact type, 'e' ending
summary: Gives an 'e' (the French feminine ending) for certain artifact types, and nothing for all others.
details: The 'e' is given for animal hides, every armour kind, axe, brooch, dagger, goblet, jug, mace, panacea, philosopher's stone, ring, spear, sword and tapestry. Any other type gives an empty text. The game's own comment on the similar FR_E calls this kind of ending the 'blessé / blessée' pair. Runs on an artifact.

label: Faith word by gender
summary: For a female character gives the adjective of her faith, for anyone else the name of an adherent of the faith.
details: The female text is the faith's adjective and the male text is the faith's adherent name (both without tooltips). The male text is also the fallback. Runs on a character.

label: Artifact type, 'le' form
summary: Gives the French article that goes before an artifact's type name: 'la ', 'l’' or 'le '.
details: Animal hides, axe, brooch, ring, spear, dagger, goblet, jug, mace, panacea, philosopher's stone and tapestry get 'la '. The armour kinds, bow, composite, elixir, longbow, pedestal, regalia, scientific apparatus and sword get 'l’'. Any other type gets 'le '. FR_Du_ArtifactType uses the same groups for 'de la ', 'de l’' and 'du '. Runs on an artifact.

label: Scheme action phrase
summary: Gives the French phrase that names a scheme's action, such as 'Enlever ...' for an abduction.
details: There is one phrase for each of 13 scheme types (abduct, befriend, claim throne, convert to witchcraft, courting, elope, fabricate hook, learn language, murder, overthrow regent, seduce, steal back artifact, sway). The plain version names the scheme's target after the verb. The '_you' version is used when the target of the scheme is the local player, for example 'Vous enlever'. Any other scheme type gets the fallback, which is the scheme's action name followed by its target. Runs on a scheme.

label: 'À' before character, by rank
summary: Gives the French 'to the' word ('au ', 'à l’', 'à la ' or 'à ') that fits the character's rank, for use before their title or name.
details: It follows the same checks as FR_le_Char. A head of faith and a character holding a title of at least barony tier (or whose spouse does) get 'au ' if male and 'à la ' if female. A group of special titles, for example emperor, archduke of Austria, emir and some religious offices, gets 'à l’'. Anyone else gets the fallback 'à '. The entry FR_au appears twice in the list. Runs on a character.

label: 'À' before landless character
summary: Gives 'au ' for a man or 'à la ' for a woman who holds no landed title, and otherwise defers to FR_au_Char.
details: The check is whether the character holds a landed title. Without one, a male character gets 'au ' and a female one 'à la '. Anyone who holds a landed title gets the result of FR_au_Char. Runs on a character.

label: 'À' before royal family member
summary: Gives the French 'to the' word for princes, princesses and similar royal family members, and otherwise defers to FR_au_Char.
details: The game's comments name the cases: a queen mother gets 'à la ', an Infant or Infante and an empress mother get 'à l’', a prince gets 'au ' and a princess gets 'à la '. A prince or princess is a character without a kingdom-tier title whose parent holds (or held) a title of kingdom tier or higher, under a feudal or clan government. Anyone else gets the result of FR_au_Char. Runs on a character.

label: 'À' before character, if landed
summary: Uses FR_au_Char_P when the character or one of their spouses holds a landed title, and FR_au_Char otherwise.
details: It gives no words of its own, it only chooses between the two other texts. Runs on a character.

label: 'À' before character, player skipped
summary: Gives 'à ' when the character is the local player, and otherwise the result of FR_au_Char_P.
details: The check is whether the character is the player's own character. Runs on a character.

label: 'À' before character, player and landed
summary: Gives 'à ' for the local player, FR_au_Char_P when the character or a spouse holds a landed title, and FR_au_Char for anyone else.
details: The checks run in that order: the local player first, then a landed title held by the character or a spouse. Runs on a character.

label: 'Du' before character, by rank
summary: Gives the French 'of the' word ('du ', 'de l’', 'de la ' or 'de ') that fits the character's rank, for use before their title or name.
details: It follows the same checks as FR_le_Char. A head of faith and a character holding a title of at least barony tier (or whose spouse does) get 'du ' if male and 'de la ' if female. A group of special titles, for example emperor, archduke of Austria, emir and some religious offices, gets 'de l’'. Anyone else gets the fallback 'de '. The entry FR_du appears twice in the list. Runs on a character.

label: Gender suffix template
summary: Picks the key prefix 'FR_female_' for a female character and 'FR_male_' for a male one, so that other French texts can build their gendered endings on it.
details: The game's own comment says all the basic gendered French character commands are based on it. Both prefixes are empty texts on their own. With two characters (Custom2) the female prefix is used only when both are female. Runs on a character.

label: 'Le' before character, by rank
summary: Gives the French article ('le ', 'la ', 'l’' or nothing) that fits the character's rank, for use before their title or name.
details: A head of faith gets 'le '. A group of special titles, for example emperor, archduke of Austria, emir and some religious offices, gets 'l’'. A character holding a title of at least barony tier (or whose spouse does) gets 'le ' if male and 'la ' if female. Anyone else gets an empty text. The entry FR_le appears twice in the list. Runs on a character.

label: 'Le' before landless character
summary: Gives 'le ' for a man or 'la ' for a woman who holds no landed title, and otherwise defers to FR_le_Char.

details: The game's comments name the cases: a queen mother gets 'la ', an Infant or Infante and an empress mother get 'l’', a prince gets 'le ' and a princess gets 'la '. Anyone else gets the result of FR_le_Char. Runs on a character.

details: It gives no words of its own, it only chooses between the two other texts. Runs on a character.

label: 'Le' before character, player skipped
summary: Gives an empty text when the character is the local player, and otherwise the result of FR_le_Char_P.
details: The check is whether the character is the player's own character, who gets no article. Runs on a character.

label: 'Le' before character, player and landed
summary: Gives an empty text for the local player, FR_le_Char_P when the character or a spouse holds a landed title, and FR_le_Char for anyone else.
details: The checks run in that order: the local player first, then a landed title held by the character or a spouse. Runs on a character.

label: Fate god name
summary: Gives the name of a faith's fate god, with one entry for each religion.
details: The entry is chosen by the faith's religion (36 entries, for example Christianity, Buddhism, Germanic, Hellenism, Islam, Slavic and Zoroastrianism). The input shows no texts, so the actual names are not known here. The meaning of 'Cel' in the key is not stated. Runs on a faith.

label: Favorite treat
summary: Gives the name of a sweet treat, such as comfit, nougat, marzipan or gingerbread, in lower case.
details: There are 18 treats. If the character has a variable favorite_treat, the matching treat is used; without that variable every treat is possible and one is picked at random. The first four texts are comfit, roasted almonds, nougat and marzipan. The rest include sweetroll, poached pear, pudding, apple tart, strawberry compote, gingerbread, fig pie and baked banana. Runs on a character.

label: Favorite treat (spoken)
summary: Gives a treat in the form vanilla uses in speech, such as 'I've made you some ...'.
details: It picks the treat the same way as FavoriteTreat, by the character's favorite_treat variable, or at random if there is none. Two entries differ from FavoriteTreat: it has treat_sweetrolls and treat_poached_pears where FavoriteTreat has treat_sweetroll and treat_poached_pear. Vanilla events use it for a grandmother offering treats. The texts for the first four treats are the same as in FavoriteTreat. Runs on a character.

label: Favorite treat (capitalised)
summary: Gives the name of a sweet treat with capital letters, such as Comfit or Roasted Almonds.
details: It mirrors FavoriteTreat with 18 entries ending in '_uppercase', picked the same way. Vanilla uses it in the title of a book artifact. Runs on a character.

label: Female or male
summary: Gives the word 'female' or 'male', matching the character's gender.
details: A female character gets gender_female ('female') and a male one gets gender_male ('male'). Runs on a character.

label: Fertility god name
summary: Gives the name of a faith's fertility god, with one entry for each religion or faith.
details: The entry is chosen by the faith's religion, with a few set by the faith itself: the Catholic and Orthodox faiths share the west_christian entry. There are 46 entries (for example Christianity, Buddhism, Vajrayana, Hinduism, Shaivism, Islam and Zoroastrianism); manicheanism appears twice. The input shows no texts, so the actual names are not known here. The meaning of 'Cel' in the key is not stated. Runs on a faith.

label: Fist or fists
summary: Gives 'fist' for a maimed character and 'fists' for anyone else.
details: The check is whether the character has the maimed trait: with it, fistfists_fist ('fist') is used, otherwise fistfists_fists ('fists'). So a sentence can speak of the one remaining fist. Runs on a character.

label: 'A' for a maimed character
summary: Gives 'a ' (with a trailing space) for a maimed character and nothing for anyone else.
details: The check is whether the character has the maimed trait. It goes with FistFists, which gives 'fist' or 'fists' by the same check, so the text can read 'a fist' or 'fists'. Runs on a character.

label: Foot or feet
summary: Gives 'foot' for a one-legged character and 'feet' for anyone else.
details: The check is whether the character has the one_legged trait: with it, footfeet_foot ('foot') is used, otherwise footfeet_feet ('feet'). Runs on a character.

label: Form of address for ruler
summary: Gives the way a subject addresses this character as their ruler, such as 'Your Majesty', 'Your Holiness' or 'my lord'.
details: The entry depends on the character's highest title tier, government, whether they are clergy, their prestige level and their gender. For example, rulers of duchy tier or below get 'my lord/lady'; independent rulers of empire tier or above get 'Your Majesty'; a Christian head of faith gets 'Your Holiness'; governors get 'Your Excellency' or 'Excellency'; clergy get 'my liege, reverend mother/father'; landless adventurers get 'captain'. There are 32 entries; several more styles exist for tribal, nomadic and other governments. Some texts contain other game texts, for example 'my [lady/lord]'. It is marked random valid, so when more than one entry fits, one is picked at random. The entries your_excellency and liege_title are each listed twice. Vanilla events use it in speech to the player's ruler. Runs on a character.

label: Formal compliment adjective
summary: Gives a flattering adjective that fits the character, such as great, venerable, pious, noble, stately or elegant.
details: There are 54 entries, most with a '_female' and a plain version that read the same in the shown texts. Each has a condition: for example great, magnanimous and worshipful need prestige level 3, noble level 2, venerable an age of 55 or more, pious a high piety level or a theocratic government, elegant good intrigue, stately high stewardship, gracious, affable and amiable a benevolent personality, and puissant a warrior with high martial. It is marked random valid, so one fitting adjective is picked at random. Vanilla uses it in front of a name, as in 'under glorious ...'. Runs on a character.

label: Former job story
summary: Gives a short first-person begging story of someone who used to hold a court position and lost it.
details: There are seven entries: court tutor, royal architect, cupbearer, court poet, chronicler, wet nurse and antiquarian. The entry follows a character flag such as royal_architect_court_position (some also fit a camp officer flag). The text sets up its own saved scope former_employer, a ruler of a larger dynasty, found near the character's location. It also uses scope:location and the game's text codes for house name, titled name and pronouns. Runs on a character.

label: Fortified building
summary: Gives the word for the character's fortified home: encampment, kasbah, durga, kastron, compound, stronghold or castle.
details: The choice follows government and culture: encampment for a landless adventurer government, kasbah for a culture with Arabic as its language, durga for Indo-Aryan heritage, kastron for Greek language, compound for a governor under a celestial government, and stronghold for a tribal government. Anyone else gets castle (the fallback). The kastron text is a glossary link. Runs on a character.

label: Food pet name
summary: Gives a sweet pet name or food word, such as songbird, rose, sunshine, honey or lemon.
details: There are 12 entries: pet names (songbird, rose, sunshine, spring blossom, petal, honeycomb) and food words (honey, berry, cilantro, lemon, almond, salt). None has a condition, and the entry is picked at random. The input shows texts only for the first four. Vanilla uses it in front of a street food name. Runs on a character.

label: Holy war name
summary: Gives the name of a great holy war waged for a faith: Crusade, Jihad, Great Purification or a general name.
details: The entry follows the faith's religion: Christianity gives ghw_crusade ('Crusade'), Islam and Yazidism give ghw_jihad, many other religions (for example Buddhism, Hinduism, Taoism and Zoroastrianism) give ghw_purification ('Great Purification'), and any other religion gets ghw_great_holy_war (the fallback). There are 15 entries in all. Runs on a faith.

label: Permanent injury phrase
summary: Gives a phrase for the lasting injury the character has, such as 'lost her leg', 'lost his eye' or 'became a eunuch'.
details: The game checks in this order: one_legged (lost leg), one_eyed (lost eye), blind (lost sight), each in a 'her' and a 'his' version by gender, then being a eunuch, then the maimed trait ('was maimed'). If none fits, the fallback is 'gained permanent scars'. Runs on a character.

label: Game over message
summary: Gives the opening line of the game over window, depending on how the character's line ended.
details: A character who is alive but no longer a ruler gets 'has lost all of their titles and became landless'. A character whose primary title is a barony gets 'has lost all but their barony titles'. Anyone else gets 'Your lineage has come to an end'. The first two use the character's full name and pronouns. Runs on a character.

label: Game over duration
summary: Gives how long the story has gone on in the game over window, such as 'For centuries you have followed ...'.
details: It measures the years since the start of the game: 200 or more gives centuries, 100 to 199 'over a century', 20 to 99 decades, 10 to 19 'over a decade', 2 to 9 years, over 1 and under 2 a year, and 1 or less a single year. The four shown texts each end with the lineage text from GameOverMessageLineage. It is marked random valid. Runs on a character.

label: Game over dynasty prestige
summary: Describes how prestigious the character's dynasty became, from legendary down to insignificant, in the game over window.
details: The entry follows the dynasty's prestige level: the maximum level gives 'legendary prestige, respected by all', then high, medium and low steps, and a minimum step. A short low version is used when the game is one year old or less, and a separate text covers a character with no dynasty. The input shows the first four texts. It is marked random valid. Runs on a character.

label: Game over lineage
summary: Names what the player followed: 'the dynasty of X', 'the X' for an organization, or 'this story'.
details: A character with a dynasty gets the dynasty text, one without a dynasty but with an organization gets the organization text, and anyone else gets 'this story'. It is used inside the duration text of the game over window. Runs on a character.

label: Game over achievements
summary: Gives a line praising one notable thing the character's dynasty achieved, such as restoring an empire or creating a kingdom.
details: There are 28 entries, one per achievement: restored empires (Roman, Carolingian, Holy Roman, Cornwall, Vasconia), unifications (Spanish, Slavs, Burgundy, Italy, Africa and more) and created kingdoms or empires (Portugal, Bosnia, Armenia, Siam, Brunei, Israel, Switzerland, Austria, Aragon and more). An entry applies when a global variable for that feat exists and the character's dynasty is the dynasty that achieved it. The four shown texts start with a space, speak to the player ('Due to you ...') and use title names in the form $h_roman_empire$. Runs on a character.

label: Lowly servant type
summary: Gives the name of a lowly household servant, such as stable boy, page, scullery maid or chandler.
details: There are 11 entries. Some fit only men (stable boy, page, chandler), some only women (scullery maid, launderer, scullion), and some any gender (scalder, saucerer, naperer, pantler). Several also need the character to be landed, landless administrative or theocratic. The plain 'servant' counts about a third as much as the others. It is marked random valid, so one fitting entry is picked at random. Runs on a character.

label: General temperament
summary: Gives a feeling word that fits the character's personality: anger, disappointment, hesitation or horror.
details: Anger fits malicious, dominant or extroverted personalities, disappointment benevolent ones, hesitation introverted, submissive or levelheaded ones, and horror emotional ones. Runs on a character.

label: Poem opening couplet
summary: Builds the first two lines of a rhyming poem, from the theme the poem has.
details: There are 15 entries: romance, mourning, legacy, strife and incompetence, three each. The entries of the theme stored in the character's variable poetry_theme fit, and one of them is picked at random. Every entry is emphasised text made of an A line and a B line (from the matching GeneratePoem_Intro_Rhyming_..._A and _B texts) split by a line break. The poem is about the character stored in the variable poem_subject. Runs on a character.

label: Poem: incompetence 1, line A
summary: First line of the opening couplet of an incompetence poem, version 1: 'A lord is nought without wisdom,'.
details: All three entries point to the first one, so the line is always the same. It uses the poem subject's title word (lord or lady).

label: Poem: incompetence 1, line B
summary: Second line of the opening couplet of an incompetence poem, version 1, in three variants ending in 'vision', 'unstricken' or 'schism'.
details: One of the three lines is picked at random. The first variant uses the subject's 'her' or 'his'.

label: Poem: incompetence 2, line A
summary: First line of the opening couplet of an incompetence poem, version 2: 'Some men simply make all others queasy,' (men or women by the subject's gender).
details: All three entries point to the first one, so the line is always the same.

label: Poem: incompetence 2, line B
summary: Second line of the opening couplet of an incompetence poem, version 2, in three variants that rhyme with 'queasy' (easy, wheezy, freely).
details: One of the three lines is picked at random. They mock the subject's appearance and breathing, or say that no one around them can talk freely.

label: Poem: incompetence 3, line A
summary: First line of the opening couplet of an incompetence poem, version 3: 'Sometimes Fate is far too cruel,'.
details: All three entries point to the first one, so the line is always the same.

label: Poem: incompetence 3, line B
summary: Second line of the opening couplet of an incompetence poem, version 3, in three variants that rhyme with 'cruel' (rule, cesspool, mule).
details: One of the three lines is picked at random. The third variant names the subject's crown with their title word (lord or lady).

label: Poem: legacy 1, line A
summary: First line of the opening couplet of a legacy poem, version 1: 'The mightiest men must leave this Earth,' (men or women by gender).
details: All three entries point to the first one, so the line is always the same.

label: Poem: legacy 1, line B
summary: Second line of the opening couplet of a legacy poem, version 1, in three variants that rhyme with 'Earth' (worth, dearth, birth).
details: One of the three lines is picked at random. They speak of the subject's deeds and realms.

label: Poem: legacy 2, line A
summary: First line of the opening couplet of a legacy poem, version 2: 'Men need not fear as lives depart,' with a capital first letter.
details: All three entries point to the first one, so the line is always the same. The subject's word for men or women starts the line, so it is capitalised.

label: Poem: legacy 2, line B
summary: Second line of the opening couplet of a legacy poem, version 2, in three variants that rhyme with 'depart' (art, heart, apart).
details: One of the three lines is picked at random.

label: Poem: legacy 3, line A
summary: First line of the opening couplet of a legacy poem, version 3: 'What man does not hope to rest when tired,' (man or woman by gender).
details: All three entries point to the first one, so the line is always the same.

label: Poem: legacy 3, line B
summary: Second line of the opening couplet of a legacy poem, version 3, in three variants that end on a question and rhyme with 'tired' (acquired, desired, retired).
details: One of the three lines is picked at random. The first and third use the subject's 'her' or 'his'; the third starts with it, so it is capitalised.

label: Poem: mourning 1, line A
summary: First line of the opening couplet of a mourning poem, version 1: 'No matter how many days twist and pass,'.
details: All three entries point to the first one, so the line is always the same.

label: Poem: mourning 1, line B
summary: Second line of the opening couplet of a mourning poem, version 1, in three variants that rhyme with 'pass' (morass, glass, grass).
details: One of the three lines is picked at random. The first uses the subject as 'her' or 'him'.

label: Poem: mourning 2, line A
summary: First line of the opening couplet of a mourning poem, version 2: 'When such beautiful countenance is hid from sight,'.
details: All three entries point to the first one, so the line is always the same.

label: Poem: mourning 2, line B
summary: Second line of the opening couplet of a mourning poem, version 2, in three variants that rhyme with 'sight' (might, slight, blight).
details: One of the three lines is picked at random.

label: Poem: mourning 3, line A
summary: First line of the opening couplet of a mourning poem, version 3: 'How cruel a mistress is random chance,'.
details: All three entries point to the first one, so the line is always the same.

label: Poem: mourning 3, line B
summary: Second line of the opening couplet of a mourning poem, version 3, in three variants that rhyme with 'chance' (dance, glance, trance).
details: One of the three lines is picked at random. The second uses the subject as 'her' or 'him'.

label: Poem: romance 1, line A
summary: First line of the opening couplet of a romance poem, version 1: 'O how such a beautiful countenance gleams,'.
details: All three entries point to the first one, so the line is always the same.

label: Poem: romance 1, line B
summary: Second line of the opening couplet of a romance poem, version 1, in three variants that rhyme with 'gleams' (dreams, seams, sunbeams).
details: One of the three lines is picked at random. The third uses the subject's 'her' or 'his'.

label: Poem: romance 2, line A
summary: First line of the opening couplet of a romance poem, version 2: 'That scrumptious woman who charms me so,' (woman or man by gender).
details: All three entries point to the first one, so the line is always the same.

label: Poem: romance 2, line B
summary: Second line of the opening couplet of a romance poem, version 2, in three variants that rhyme with 'so' (go, glow, owe).
details: One of the three lines is picked at random. The first asks where the subject went, using woman or man by gender.

label: Poem: romance 3, line A
summary: First line of the opening couplet of a romance poem, version 3: 'I wonder what secrets her mask protects?' (her or his by gender).
details: All three entries point to the first one, so the line is always the same.

label: Poem: romance 3, line B
summary: Second line of the opening couplet of a romance poem, version 3, in three variants that rhyme with 'protects' (subjects, defects, affect).
details: One of the three lines is picked at random. The second uses woman or man by gender.

label: Poem: strife 1, line A
summary: First line of the opening couplet of a war poem, version 1: 'When red-plumed war comes to her lands,' (her or his by gender).
details: All three entries point to the first one, so the line is always the same.

label: Poem: strife 1, line B
summary: Second line of the opening couplet of a war poem, version 1, in three variants that rhyme with 'lands' (hands, firebrand, demands).
details: One of the three lines is picked at random.

label: Poem: strife 2, line A
summary: First line of the opening couplet of a war poem, version 2: 'Where other men speak silvered words,' (men or women by gender).
details: All three entries point to the first one, so the line is always the same.

label: Poem: strife 2, line B
summary: Second line of the opening couplet of a war poem, version 2, in three variants that rhyme with 'words' (girds, herds, turds).
details: One of the three lines is picked at random. The first calls the subject a hero or heroine in iron (using a custom text for hero/heroine and a reflexive 'herself' or 'himself'), the second says they lead soldiers, and the last is crude.

label: Poem: strife 3, line A
summary: First line of the opening couplet of a war poem, version 3: 'Though conflict brings wrath to all someday,'.
details: All three entries point to the first one, so the line is always the same.

label: Poem: strife 3, line B
summary: Second line of the opening couplet of a war poem, version 3, in three variants that rhyme with 'someday' (bay, fray, prey).
details: One of the three lines is picked at random. The first uses woman or man by gender, the second a custom text for hero or heroine, and the third a possessive form of hero or heroine.

label: Poem closing couplet
summary: Builds the last two lines of a rhyming poem, from the theme the poem has.
details: There are 15 entries: romance, mourning, legacy, strife and incompetence, three each. The entries of the theme stored in the character's variable poetry_theme fit, and one of them is picked at random. Every entry is emphasised text made of an A line and a B line (from the matching GeneratePoem_Outro_Rhyming_..._A and _B texts) split by a line break. It is the closing partner of GeneratePoem_Intro_Rhyming.

label: Poem end: incompetence 1, line A
summary: First line of the closing couplet of an incompetence poem, version 1: 'Oh what cruel fates Destiny doles out,'.
details: All three entries point to the first one, so the line is always the same.
